newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds slip on rate fears; dollar weaker.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds slip on rate fears; dollar weaker.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Friday on worries that the strong dollar would hurt U.S. exports, while bonds slid on expectations the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week.
The dollar fell after comments by a top Fed official raised concerns that the United States may not tolerate a further appreciation of the currency.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed 15.49 points lower at 6,804.79. For the week, it lost 130.67 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,241 to 1,154 on active volume of 534 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Wall Streeters worried the strong dollar was eroding the profit picture of multinationals, and they focused on Eastman Kodak Co., which tumbled 9-1/4 to 79 and International Business Machines Corp., off 4-3/8 to 132-1/2, in consolidated trading.
For some time, analysts have cautioned that multinationals would begin to suffer from the strong currency. With concrete evidence now emerging, they said the concerns could become more widespread.

"Often this starts with somebody signalling to the investment community that there may be a problem," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "Then, it starts to become less specific."

U.S. Treasuries ended down 4/32 at 95-23/32, to yield 6.97 percent, up from to 6.96 percent Thursday. Even amid lackluster trading, expectation abounded that the Fed will tighten monetary policy next week.

Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc., said there was little, if any, market reaction to a Johnson-Smick International report saying there was still only a 50-50 chance the Fed would tighten, or raise interest rates, next week.
"I agree only ... that you can't say with 100 percent certainty that the Fed will move next week," Flanagan said. "There's more certainty that the Fed will move by Memorial Day."
The dollar slid to 1.6853 German marks in late trading from 1.6930 marks late Thursday. The dollar fell to 122.85 Japanese yen from 123.73 yen.

The U.S. currency was affected by a news report that Fed Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin said Treasury Secretary Robert Ribin set limits on his strong dollar policy. The Fed denied Rivlin made the remarks.

In commodity markets, pork futures soared the daily trading limit for a second straight day on furious buying from speculators and commercial firms who believe pork exports will jump due to Taiwan's exit from the world market.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, May pork belly futures closed up the 3-cent-a-pound daily limit at 79.300 cents and June lean hogs up the 2-cent-a-pound limit at 80.150 cents.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain prices closed lower as speculation grew that Taiwan would sharply cut back on feed imports as it culls its diseased swine herd.
May corn closed down 4-1/2 cents a bushel at $3.00-1/4.
May soybeans fell 9-1/2 cents a bushel to $8.42-1/2.
Wheat prices also fell on worries about U.S. prices being too high for foreign buyers. May wheat closed 7-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $3.90.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index ended 3.3 points lower at 4,254.8, falling 169.5 from a week ago. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average added 139.45 points, or 0.75 percent, to finish at 18,633.16.
